source.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
source.authors: David Bau; Bo-Lei Zhou; A. Khosla; A. Oliva; A. Torralba

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures visual-unit interpretability with network dissection and compares it across CNN architectures and training conditions. This is a different method and model domain from the claim's Qwen neuron-pole audit.
record.gate_note: The paper's results relevant to V4 include architecture comparisons, regularization comparisons, and a human evaluation of network dissection's interpretations. It also reports many other results (for example, self-supervised-task comparisons and transfer accuracy) that do not test the listed claim versions. The architecture comparison is reported as an ordering in the text, while its plotted counts are not numerically stated. Human-evaluation denominator counts are included in row notes rather than treated as separate outcomes.
record.test_reason: Network dissection scores CNN units against labeled visual concepts and compares them across architectures and training conditions. This bears on V4's claim that architecture and regularization, not inherent mess, determine unit interpretability. The method, measure (unique-detector counts) and domain (vision CNNs) differ from the essay's.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that interpretability is axis-aligned (destroyed by rotation without changing discriminative power), consistent with partially disentangled representations. They also find that layers disentangle different concept categories and that architecture and training techniques (e.g., batch norm) significantly affect interpretability. The human-comparability claim applies to conv5 only.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses thresholded CNN activation maps and pixel-wise visual-concept annotations to score unit/concept alignment; it does not use language-model explanations tested on held-out neuron activations or the Qwen neuron-pole rating procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability varies with architecture, training dataset, dropout, and batch normalization. The paper also reports differences across convolutional layers in the human evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: Random rotation of AlexNet conv5 reduces unique detectors by 80% with identical discriminative power; interpretability falls as the rotation grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual units form a privileged, axis-aligned basis: interpretable units are not equally found along random directions.

record.problems: The interpretation measure depends on the Broden concept set and the paper notes that concepts absent from Broden may not score well. Human evaluation uses 15 images per unit, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the relevant results. Some comparisons are available only as plots without numerical values. The study concerns visual CNNs, not language models.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows omitted. Other experiments, including self-supervised task comparisons, training-iteration plots, and action40 transfer accuracy, do not test the listed versions.

untested.parts: Language models, dense vs MoE, scaling to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization (Fig. 6 notes GoogLeNet units on horses+dogs but does not analyse them).

Whether better explanation tools raise the interpretable share. The essay's ~5% to ~99% estimates for InceptionV1-sized models. Shares, as opposed to counts, of interpretable units across architectures.
Neuron attribution graphs and replacement-model reconstruction error.
Whether activating-example explanations predict firing on new inputs.

missing.what: Width experiment: AlexNet-GAP-Wide (768 conv5 units) has many more unique detectors and detector units than standard AlexNet at ~0.5% lower accuracy. Going to 1024/2048 units does not significantly increase unique concepts further. This bears on the architecture-vs-capacity part of V4.
Random-rotation result: 80% fewer unique detectors after rotation, decreasing with rotation angle. Context for whether units are the natural basis.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its interpretability measure counts unique Broden concepts matched by units at IoU > 0.04. That count depends on the concept set and on the number of units, so it is not the per-neuron share V4 refers to. Rows r1–r5 are method validation and were unlinked. Dataset and initialization rows were unlinked as not naming V4's causes.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron poles and the reported one-job, two-related-jobs, and not-understood shares.
Language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, and scaling up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization.

The paper does not compare explanation tools, test whether better tools raise interpretability, or assess the essay's InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates of about 5% to about 99%. Its CNN results do not establish the claim for modern language models.
Attribution graphs, behavioural reconstruction, and replacement models.
Whether explanations fit on activating examples predict where neurons fire on new examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: CNN architectures: AlexNet, GoogLeNet, VGG, and ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of unique visual-concept detectors in the last convolutional layer across architectures.
rows.value: Interpretability ordering reported as ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet.
rows.note: The paper describes the architecture ordering in the text; numerical detector counts are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: Observed in direction only. The measure is a count of unique concepts, not a share of interpretable units. Deeper nets also have many more last-layer units (ResNet 2048 vs AlexNet 256), so the ordering is confounded with width. No numbers are given in the text.

source_check.problem: Text gives ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet by unique detectors at the last conv layer. Counts appear only in the figure.

rows.subject: CNNs trained on Places and ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared unique-detector counts across training datasets.
rows.note: This is the paper's stated aggregate comparison; the plotted numerical counts are not given in the text.
rows.check: Compares training datasets (Places vs ImageNet), which is not architecture, regularization or tools as V4 names.

rows.subject: Places205-AlexNet without dropout
rows.operation_detail: Measured detector counts after removing dropout from the fully connected layers.
rows.baseline: Places205-AlexNet baseline with dropout; figure only
rows.value: More texture detectors than the baseline; numerical value figure only.
rows.note: The paper states that removing dropout yields more texture detectors.
rows.check: Dropout removal shifts the category mix (more textures). It does not show overall interpretability rising or falling.

rows.subject: Places205-AlexNet without dropout
rows.operation_detail: Measured detector counts after removing dropout from the fully connected layers.
rows.baseline: Places205-AlexNet baseline with dropout; figure only
rows.value: Fewer object detectors than the baseline; numerical value figure only.
rows.note: The paper states that removing dropout yields fewer object detectors.
rows.check: Dropout removal yields fewer object detectors but more texture detectors. The net interpretability change is not stated, so 'partial' is unfounded.

rows.subject: Places205-AlexNet with batch normalization
rows.operation_detail: Measured interpretability after applying batch normalization at each convolutional layer.
rows.baseline: Places205-AlexNet baseline; numerical value figure only
rows.value: Batch normalization decreases interpretability significantly; numerical value figure only.
rows.note: The paper describes a significant decrease. It reports top-1 validation accuracy of 50.5% for BatchNorm versus 50.0% for the baseline, but that accuracy is not the interpretability measure.
rows.check: A training/normalization choice significantly lowers interpretability at equal accuracy. This is consistent with V4's regularization cause, but BatchNorm is itself a modern component. The value is figure-only.

source_check.problem: Text says BatchNorm 'seems to decrease interpretability significantly'. Top-1 is 50.5% vs 50.0%, as stated. Counts appear only in the figure.

tranche.reason: A different method (Network Dissection on CNNs) aimed at the same question: what drives unit interpretability across architectures and training conditions.

source_check.notes: All counts are figure-only (Figs. 7, 11). Table 3 gives a human-rated share of interpretable AlexNet units per layer (conv5 194/256), which is not in the rows. The per-unit ratio and the large-network warning in V4.against[5] are not in this CVPR text. The paper calls dropout and BN training techniques and 'regularizations'.

statements.correction: CVPR text: ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet by unique detectors at the last conv layer (ImageNet and Places). Authors: deeper architectures 'appear to allow greater interpretability'. Values in Fig. 7 only.
statements.problem: The CVPR ordering is right for this study. The paraphrase drops the authors' hedge: they say deeper architectures 'appear to allow greater interpretability'. The width confound is the verdict's reading. The TPAMI ordering belongs to 1711.05611.

What it says about this study matches the text. BatchNorm lowers interpretability significantly (top-1 50.5% vs 50.0% baseline). Removing FC dropout gives more texture and fewer object detectors. The other numbers belong to other studies.

statements.correction: This text gives only counts of unique detectors (Fig. 7), with no per-unit ratio and no warning about large networks. Sec. 3.7: widening AlexNet conv5 from 256 to 768 units gives many more unique detectors. 1024 or 2048 units give no significant further rise.
statements.problem: Count-not-share is right: the measure is the number of unique detectors. This CVPR text has no per-unit ratio, no VGG-highest-by-ratio ranking and no authors' warning that the count favors large networks. These likely come from the TPAMI extension 1711.05611, not from this study's r6.
This study gives no share estimate for InceptionV1 or ConvNeXt. GoogLeNet appears only in the count ranking (this study's r6 as well as 1711.05611).
No old-vs-new tool share comparison. Table 3 checks Network Dissection labels against human labels on AlexNet layers (conv5: 194/256 interpretable, ND 71% vs human 91%), as the statement notes.
BatchNorm lowering interpretability is right for this study. The paper frames BN as a training technique and a 'regularization' (Fig. 11 caption), not an architecture.

For this study, BatchNorm lowers interpretability at roughly equal accuracy, and removing dropout shifts detectors toward textures and away from objects. The verdict filing (limits_scope) is described correctly.
Matches the text. Places205 AlexNet conv5 has 80% fewer unique detectors after a random rotation, with identical discriminative power, and interpretability falls as α grows (Fig. 4).
